extracted.intended_audience: tech and AI company executives, product, marketing, and legal/compliance teams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, auditing, and defending marketing statements about AI-powered products and services to avoid FTC enforcement and consumer deception. Focuses especially on claims affecting children, deepfakes/synthetic media, and substantiation requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful and Substantiated Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Every claim about what AI can do must be truthful, substantiated, and clearly framed so that reasonable consumers—including parents—are not misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be based on current performance data, not future ambitions; supported by internal testing, documentation, or third‑party validation. If you cannot back up a claim today, revise, qualify, or remove it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Magic Word' AI Implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'AI' as a marketing 'magic word' that implies advanced, almost superhuman capabilities without solid evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of implying capabilities that are not actually delivered; common risky formulations include promises of guaranteed outcomes or overstated automation. Replace vague 'AI' hype with concrete, evidence‑backed feature descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy, Safety, and Performance Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious when making claims about accuracy, safety, or performance of AI tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid guarantees (e.g., specific revenue boosts or perfect compliance). Provide performance metrics and limitations where appropriate; do not claim detection/removal of all harmful content or bias if performance does not support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Unvalidated Expert‑Level Advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid marketing AI as providing expert‑level advice (such as legal or medical) unless the system is validated, monitored, and appropriately staffed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If AI interfaces with professional domains, include clear disclaimers, scope limits, and human oversight; do not imply the system replaces licensed professionals unless substantiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, Prominent Disclosures (Not Fine Print)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures and disclaimers about AI use must be crystal clear and not buried in fine print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label synthetic content and explain limitations and data use plainly and prominently so a reasonable consumer would understand; tailor prominence to the context and audience (parents, kids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Represent Synthetic Media as Real
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting AI‑generated or doctored media (deepfakes, synthetic videos/audio/images) in a way a reasonable consumer would interpret as real footage, testimony, or endorsements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using synthetic content, clearly label it as artificial; avoid impersonating real people or creating fabricated endorsements; establish internal review processes to vet synthetic content before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Quiet Use of AI in Professional Contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not quietly use AI in contexts where consumers assume interaction with trained professionals (e.g., health or mental health support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose when interactions are with AI rather than a human professional, and limit claims that suggest professional qualification or therapeutic efficacy absent validation and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child‑Sensitive Design and Messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: If kids or teens may interact with the AI tool, treat the product as high priority for enhanced controls and messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement robust age gates and parental controls that match the real audience; design chatbot behavior and filters to avoid romantic/sexual or self‑harm content; craft clear, prominent disclosures explaining AI capabilities and data practices for minors.

rubrics_metrics.name: COPPA and Child Privacy Obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: AI products that track, profile, or personalize experiences for children can trigger COPPA and state privacy laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using kids' data for training, evaluation, or personalization, ensure a legal basis and parental consent structures; do not hide behind generic privacy policies or ambiguous age gating if the audience skews young.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map and Audit All AI Representations Across Channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Audit every representation you make about AI across website copy, app store listings, investor decks, sales scripts, privacy policies, and other channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether each statement is factually accurate, supported by evidence, and presented so a reasonable consumer would understand it. Conduct regular audits and build substantiation files to withstand regulatory scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk Categorization and Governance Calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify AI projects into risk buckets (e.g., 'Unacceptable', 'High', 'Limited', 'Minimal') and calibrate marketing claims, disclosures, and internal controls accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High‑risk use cases (hiring, worker management, health advice) require stronger substantiation, governance, and more cautious public claims than entertainment use cases. Use classification to drive review intensity and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation Controls and Realistic Training Data
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure moderation controls and training data reflect realistic behavior of the audiences (especially teens) the product may reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators will evaluate whether moderation and data exposures are appropriate; test and document moderation efficacy and limitations, and align marketing to actual moderation performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Over‑Promising to Vulnerable Groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not market AI in ways that downplay risks to vulnerable groups (children, mental‑health sufferers, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotions that understate possible harms or overstate benefits for vulnerable groups increase regulatory and enforcement risk; make limits and safeguards explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label AI‑Generated Endorsements and Testimonials
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using AI to create or doctor endorsements/testimonials without clear labeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthetic testimonials that impersonate real customers or public figures are likely deceptive; disclose synthetic origin and do not present fabricated experiences as real consumer results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align UI/UX and External Messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the user experience and product behavior align with public-facing marketing and disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory risk increases when internal documentation shows awareness of risks but external messaging downplays or omits them. Review UI flows, funnels, and copy for consistency with actual product behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build Substantiation Files and Evidence Packages
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantiate marketing claims with testing, documentation, and third‑party validation so they can withstand regulatory scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect validation data, internal testing reports, and expert review; keep records that show the basis for performance and safety claims in case of FTC inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement Internal Review Processes for Synthetic Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish internal review and vetting processes for any synthetic media or AI‑generated content before it goes live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process should include checks for misleading context, impersonation risk, appropriate labeling, and escalation for high‑risk uses; document approvals and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit Mental‑Health and Therapy‑Style Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid marketing AI chatbots as therapeutic or mental‑health treatment absent proper oversight, disclaimers, and mechanisms to redirect users in crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominently display disclaimers, sharply limit treatment claims, and implement guardrails that escalate or refer users to professional resources when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove or Revise Problematic AI Claims Proactively
rubrics_metrics.description: Review and revise sales pages, landing pages, and marketing funnels to remove or qualify problematic AI claims before regulators do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/compliance teams should work with product and marketing to correct misleading statements quickly; prior negotiation and remediation can reduce enforcement risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful Handling of Influencer and Endorsement Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel required for endorsements, testimonials, and influencer content that involve or reference AI tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure disclosures identify material connections and synthetic alterations; influencers should not present AI outputs as verified personal experiences if not true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume Heightened Scrutiny for Teen‑Facing Features
rubrics_metrics.description: If an AI feature can reach minors, assume regulators will closely evaluate design, disclosures, and marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare to show how parental controls, age gating, moderation, and disclosures match the real audience and product behavior; document decisions and testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable‑Consumer Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate claims under the standard of whether a reasonable consumer—especially a parent—would be misled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame messaging so ordinary users can understand capabilities and limits; avoid technical obfuscation that could mislead non‑expert audiences.
